item.title: Sakoshi: A Preserved Harbour Village on the Inland Sea — Guide
item.description: Sakoshi, a small harbour village on a sheltered bay near Ako in western Hyogo, is one of the quietest and most atmospheric old townscapes on the Seto Inland Sea. It prospered in the Edo period as a port of call for the kitamaebune coastal trading ships, and that wealth built the white-plastered merchant houses, storehouses and lanes that survive along its main street today. Its landmarks are a working sake brewery that has operated here for centuries and now welcomes visitors, and the hillside Osake Shrine overlooking the bay — a rewarding, uncrowded stop for anyone drawn to old Japan.

item.title: Fukui Sake Brewery Museum: Tasting and the Craft of Local Sake — Guide
item.description: Fukui’s clean mountain water and quality locally-grown rice make it a respected sake-producing region, and a visit to a local brewery museum offers visitors an accessible look at the traditional brewing process, from rice polishing and fermentation through to bottling, often housed within a working or historic brewery building. Most brewery visits include tastings of the region’s sake, giving visitors the chance to sample different styles and grades and understand how Fukui’s natural conditions shape the character of its rice wine.

item.title: Aizu-Wakamatsu Sake: Brewery Tours & Tastings — Guide
item.description: Aizu-Wakamatsu has been one of Japan’s premier sake-brewing regions for centuries, its combination of pure mountain snowmelt water, rice-growing plains and bitterly cold winters creating ideal conditions for fermentation. Several historic breweries in and around the city, some dating back over 100 years, open their doors for tours explaining the brewing process, followed by tastings of a range of styles from dry (karakuchi) to fruity ginjo varieties, often in atmospheric wooden kura (storehouse) buildings.

item.title: Hyogo Leisure: Jazz Bars, Sake Breweries & Harbor Cruises
item.description: Kobe has always been a city that knows how to enjoy itself. Its history as Japan’s most cosmopolitan port city — open to foreign trade from 1868, home to settled European and Chinese merchant communities within a generation — left a cultural legacy that distinguishes it from every other Japanese city. The architecture is different, the food culture is different, the music is different, and the pace of an evening out carries a particular ease that visitors from Tokyo and Osaka both notice immediately.
